slides.title: Walk one request: reading a signed-in profile
slides.subtitle: How the request, identity and data move across our layers
slides.source: src/api/accounts.ts; hooks/useAccount.ts; server/api.mjs; Register.cs; AppAuthJson.cs
slides.notes: Use a profile read to explain the consequential design. Browser fetch sends GET /api/profile with an opaque HttpOnly cookie, no body token. Node looks up the 12-hour local session and selects the stored backend user token. The forwarding client supplies app_access, verified IP and a cached login-issued service admin_token. Node http(s).request can send the backend GET JSON body; browser fetch cannot. AppAuthJson validates app/IP and visitor token; Register reads user/school and returns profile data. Node projects the four permitted public fields. No password, user token or service token reaches the browser.

slides.title: UML class view: shared credentials and request inheritance
slides.subtitle: These are actual C# request types, not invented service/entity classes
slides.source: Backend/Components/AppAuthJson.cs; Controllers/Register.cs, LogIn.cs, Admin.cs
slides.notes: Explain that AppAuthJson combines body fields with static validation operations in the current code. Register.Info, LogIn.Info and Admin.Info inherit those fields. Nullable request properties support per-operation handling; they do not mean that required registration/login fields are optional at runtime. These DTOs differ from the database tables and from Node’s browser-safe TypeScript contracts. The schema model follows on separate slides. This design also exposes a coupling trade-off: validation and request shape share a class.

slides.title: UML sequence: login establishes a website session
slides.subtitle: Prepared forwarding identity is assumed; its renewal rules are covered in the appendix
slides.source: docs/uml D10; api.mjs /api/login; LogIn.Post; Register.Get
slides.notes: Time flows downward. Backend login verifies credentials/attempt admission, reuses or issues a token and returns it only to Node. Node then uses GET /Register with the token in the JSON body to obtain a public profile. Only a validated profile permits local session creation. The browser receives a projected profile and opaque HttpOnly cookie, not the backend token. The Node self-message denotes the local Map write. Backend token validity and local session validity are separate clocks. Failed login/profile read is an alternative result; it does not establish the new Map entry.

slides.title: Database core: one school, many users, optional admin membership
slides.subtitle: UML-style relational model of four declared tables; these are not ORM entity classes
slides.source: DB_Schema.txt; Register.cs; LogIn.cs; Components/Sql.cs
slides.notes: The declared account core includes Schools, User, Admins and Access_Token. User.school_id is required; an account can have zero or one Admins row and many access tokens. Email/token uniqueness matters to lookup and issuance. The schema declares RESTRICT for school/user and user/admin relationships and CASCADE for tokens, but the connection does not explicitly enable foreign keys. Do not claim these runtime effects were verified. Password and email values are deterministically reversibly encrypted in the current code, which is a security debt rather than a recommended password strategy.

slides.title: Security data: attempts are observations, not always blocks
slides.subtitle: Four more declared tables track IP identity, user/IP association and attempt windows
slides.source: DB_Schema.txt; Users.cs; IP.cs; docs/dfd P35/P43/P44
slides.notes: These complete the eight-table declared schema. Multiple historical attempt rows may exist, so draw 0..* rather than assuming a unique per-user row. User_Has_IPs has NOT NULL foreign keys and a unique pair. The active time window and count determine blocking, not merely table membership. A successful first observation can have count -1. At user threshold 10, existing tokens are revoked; clearing attempts later does not recreate them. IP blocks do not directly revoke tokens. Process-local identity locks serialize related updates but do not coordinate multiple instances.

slides.title: Three identities and two expiry clocks
slides.subtitle: Browser session, visitor token and service identity serve different purposes
slides.source: api.mjs sessions/forwarding client; AppAuthJson.ValidateApp/ValidateToken; Env.cs
slides.notes: Keep these three identities separate. se_session is an opaque cookie ID. Node maps it to the visitor access_token. Separately, a configured service account logs in and its admin access token becomes admin_token for trusted IP forwarding. Human admin authorization comes from the visitor’s own token and Admins level; it is not conferred by the service token. to_user is a selector for an eligible target while sudo_id/caller level retain provenance. Local Map expiry is 12 hours; backend ordinary/admin tokens last 21/3 days. Public school reads and login admission have different checks from token-authenticated actions.

shapes.text: Three identities and two expiry clocks
Browser session, visitor token and service identity serve different purposes

slides.title: Technology decisions: constraints, benefits and trade-offs
slides.subtitle: Protocol compatibility, client state and single-instance storage shape the design
slides.source: package.json; vite.config.ts; api.mjs; csproj; Sql.cs; render.yaml
slides.notes: Use precise reasons, not generic technology praise. React/TypeScript fits a stateful UI and explicit browser contracts. Node is consequential because browser fetch cannot send the upstream GET JSON body and shared credentials should stay off the client. ASP.NET supplies typed controller/validation infrastructure already present. SQLite fits a portable single-instance prototype but brings path, schema migration and concurrency/foreign-key obligations. Render hosting uses the existing Node manifest; Azure is the configured API destination. These explanations are inferred design fit, not a claim that a formal ADR or original team rationale exists.

slides.subtitle: Fresh checks reveal actionable defects without rewriting the application during presentation work
slides.source: src/App.test.tsx:20; App.tsx listing-grid and offer input; evidence files
slides.notes: Issue one: the test expects getByRole(list, name Sample listings), but the current ul.listing-grid has no accessible label. The fix should restore the intended accessible name, keeping a meaningful assertion, not simply deleting the test. Proposed fix: choose cent precision, positive validation and a browser test for whole-dollar and fractional values. These observations are separate from the 116 passed count. Both fixes belong in application work after this review; they were not silently applied to change the evidence.

slides.title: Appendix | three edge cases that reveal design understanding
slides.subtitle: Protocol adaptation, saved writes and qualified revocation each require distinct handling
slides.source: api.mjs upstream/forwarding/profile/logout; AppAuthJson.cs; LogIn.cs
slides.notes: Explain three non-obvious cases. Forwarding token expiry is explicitly recognized as pre-operation rejection and permits a single coalesced service-token renewal/retry; ordinary server, forbidden or visitor-expired errors do not permit replay. A committed profile write followed by a failed read returns saved status with profile null and should not silently repeat a password update. Logout returns success even on certain backend token-validation failures; the UI must not certify target revocation. These are precisely the sort of details that show the team understands its implementation, beyond the names of frameworks.
